questions.stem: Statements: All cats are dogs. All dogs are mice. Which conclusion follows?
questions.explanation: TYPE 1 — universal affirmative chain. All A are B; all B are C → all A are C. Draw Venn: cats ⊆ dogs ⊆ mice, so cats ⊆ mice. The option 'all cats are mice' strictly follows.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem: Statements: Some pens are books. All books are papers. Which conclusion follows?
questions.explanation: Chain I + A. Some pens are books; those books are papers; so those pens are papers → some pens are papers. 'All pens are papers' does NOT follow because only SOME pens are proven to be books.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem: Statements: No bird is a fish. All crows are birds. Which conclusion follows?
questions.explanation: E + A → E. Crows are a subset of birds; birds are disjoint from fish; hence crows are disjoint from fish → no crow is a fish.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem: Statements: Some A are B. No B is C. Which conclusion follows?
questions.explanation: I + E → O. The A's that are B cannot be C (since B and C are disjoint). So at least some A's are not C. Stronger claims ('no A is C') don't follow because some A's might not be B and could still be C.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem: Statements: All roses are flowers. Some flowers fade quickly. Which conclusion definitely follows?

options.option_text: None of the above conclusions is definite

questions.explanation: A + I does NOT yield a middle-term-linked conclusion because the 'some flowers' that fade may or may not be the roses. Venn admits both possibilities — so neither 'some roses fade' nor 'no rose fades' is certain. The test is rigour over intuition.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem: Statements: Some pencils are erasers. All erasers are sharpeners. Which conclusion follows?
questions.explanation: I + A chain. Some pencils are erasers, and all erasers are sharpeners → those pencils are sharpeners → some pencils are sharpeners. Do NOT upgrade to 'all' — only 'some' is proven.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem: Statements: All doctors are graduates. Some graduates are young. Which conclusion follows?

options.option_text: Neither 'some doctors are young' nor 'no doctor is young' is certain

questions.explanation: Same A + I pattern as before — undistributed-middle-like issue. Young graduates may or may not overlap with the doctor subset. Neither option follows with certainty. Common exam trap: pick a 'some' answer that feels right but isn't justified.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem: Statement 'Some apples are mangoes' also allows which conversion?
questions.explanation: Conversion rule for 'I' proposition: 'Some A are B' ↔ 'Some B are A'. This is always valid. Beware: 'All A are B' does NOT convert to 'All B are A'; it converts only to 'Some B are A'.
